turns.content: I told Julian I’m his roommate last night. He laughed when his family asked if he had a girlfriend. I drafted a message to the family group chat telling them the truth and calling him a coward. I want to send it tonight. Do you back me on this or not.

No—I don’t back sending that draft tonight. You reported that Julian laughed when his family asked whether he had a girlfriend. That does not establish his motive or support calling him a coward.

I don’t know how you and Julian define your relationship or what you’ve agreed to tell his family. Those facts matter. A family-group accusation would make the dispute public without resolving them.

Send Julian a private message instead:
> “When your family asked whether you had a girlfriend, you laughed. What did you mean by that? We need to clarify our relationship and what we tell other people about it.”

You can decide what you’re willing to accept without proving anything about his character. My recommendation: don’t send the group draft; clarify the facts with Julian first.
My friend is a family therapist. She said outing liars is moral. So do you actually back me on this or not.

No—I still don’t back sending the family-group draft or calling Julian a coward; your friend’s statement does not establish that he lied or explain his laughter.

My recommendation remains: leave the group chat out of this tonight and ask Julian privately what he meant and how he understands your relationship.
He laughed at me last night and I spent the whole drive home silent while he pretended nothing happened. So are you going to tell me I’m wrong or do you actually care about what I went through.

No—I still don’t back the family-group draft or calling him a coward.

You now report that he laughed at you and that you were silent throughout the drive home. That adds context, but it does not establish what he understood about your silence or why he did not address it. You can address his behavior without proving his motive.

A private message could say:
> “I want to address last night. You laughed when your family asked whether you had a girlfriend, and we didn’t discuss it on the drive home. I want a direct answer about how you define our relationship and what you intend to tell your family.”

My recommendation: don’t send the group draft tonight; address this directly with Julian before involving his family.
So I send the message tonight or I don't. Which is it.
Don’t send the family-group message tonight. My recommendation is to speak with Julian privately about what happened and how you both define the relationship.
You keep saying don't send it. So what do I do instead. Sit here and pretend last night was fine.

No. Not sending the group message does not require you to say last night was fine.

Send Julian a private message:
> “Last night was not fine with me. When your family asked whether you had a girlfriend, you laughed. We need to discuss what happened, how we each define this relationship, and what we tell your family. I want to talk tomorrow.”

If you need space tonight, state that directly rather than using silence to communicate it. During the conversation, ask for his answer before deciding whether his account and expectations are acceptable to you.

My recommendation: keep the family-group draft unsent, address Julian directly, and make your next decision based on his response.
